newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels free 20 hostages, 83 remain.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels free 20 hostages, 83 remain.

text.p: The Marxist rebels holding VIP hostages at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima released 20 more captives on Saturday, leaving a total of 83 inside the compound.
Wearing crumpled suits, the freed men left the fortified compound during their 11th day in captivity, walking in single-file and smiling to waiting journalists.
The freed hostages included the ambassadors of the Dominican Republic, Jose Diaz, and of Malaysia, Ahmad Mokhtar, Peruvian diplomats and Japanese businessmen.
They boarded a bus outside the residence and were driven to a nearby police hospital.

The release followed the first face-to-face contact between the rebels and a government negotiator after Peru's chief mediator, Education Minister Domingo Palermo, spent three hours and 15 minutes inside the compound earlier on Saturday.

"We have made advances for a solution in this serious incident," Palermo said moments after the hostages walked free. "We have achieved the release of 20 hostages and those that remain are in good health."

The Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels also issued a statement with the freed captives, which said they "deplored" being labeled as terrorists and did not want to be compared to Peru's larger and bloodier guerrilla group -- the Maoist Shining Path.

The guerrillas have released more than 420 hostages since storming the residence during a cocktail party on Dec 17. Before Saturday's release, negotiations with the government seemed to be at a stalemate, as the rebels had freed only three hostages since releasing a group of 225 men last Sunday.
The remaining hostages include those considered by the guerrillas as their best bargaining chips, including top Peruvian officials, the Japanese, Bolivian and Honduran ambassadors and Japanese VIPs.

The release of the Malaysian ambassdor followed the diplomatic mission of Kuala Lumpur's Foreign Minister, Abdullah Ahmad Badawi, who left Peru on Saturday after three days of talks with the Peruvian government and Red Cross mediators.
